title: The Case of the Missing Hammer
label: A Bizzing mystery
setting: Þrymskviða, the Lay of Thrym: Thor's hall, the dwarves' forge, Jötunheim and the Thing

souvenir.name: a falcon feather from Freyja's cloak

sourceText: Þrymskviða, the Lay of Thrym, in the Poetic Edda, retold; quoted lines from Henry Adams Bellows's translation (1923)

card.text:
Thor wakes in the dark, and his hammer is gone.
The door was barred. The snow outside is smooth. Nobody came in.
Without the hammer, Asgard's walls are unguarded, and by nightfall the giants will know it.
Everyone in the hall says the same name: "It's always Loki."
Is it, {det}?
A name is not evidence.

cutscene.place: The office, the evening after Case 5
cutscene.picture: The office, the evening after Case 5. Snow on the round window, though it is not snowing in Inkwell. The painted Door is ajar; frost feathers its keyhole. {det}'s persona sign is in the panel. Dev sits on the floor with a library book: Runes and Riddles of the North. DEV: "Twenty-four letters. No Y. And they carved them on sticks. I love them."

Quill, deerstalker on, a scarf on top. QUILL: "Inside a story, you can find out anything. You can't change what it is. Bring back what you learned. And mind the clock. This one keeps the dark until sunrise."

cutscene.place: Through the Door: Thor's hall, Bilskirnir, before dawn
cutscene.picture: Through the Door: Thor's hall, Bilskirnir, before dawn. A long hall of carved wood, a hearth banked high and glowing, benches, shields on the walls (painted as round shapes, no symbols). A wooden peg above the hearth, directly under a square smoke-hole in the roof. The peg is empty.

Thor, in a night-cap, both fists in the air. The roar is lettered in the poem's own words, live text: THOR: "Hear now, Loki, what now I say…" …MY HAMMER IS GONE! (Dust falls from the rafters. A goat in the stable bleats.)

cutscene.place: Every face in the hall turns to the doorway
cutscene.picture: Every face in the hall turns to the doorway, where a lean, red-haired figure has just walked in, brushing soot off his sleeve. EVERYONE: "Loki." LOKI: "Good morning to you too."

lines.text: I've read every story about him. It's *always* Loki.

cast.name: Loki
cast.look: Lean and quick, red-brown hair that will not lie flat, a green cloak with too many pockets, a grin that arrives before he does
cast.manner: Clever, charming, slippery with words; tells the truth in a way that sounds like a lie
cast.note: Motive: the gods blame him for everything, and the hammer's short handle really is his fault. · Secret: he spent the whole night at the dwarves' forge, asking them to make Thor a longer handle as a sorry-present. They said no. He is embarrassed, and he would rather be suspected than laughed at

cast.name: Brokkr and Sindri
cast.look: Two broad, short brothers in leather aprons, beards singed at the ends, soot to the elbows; Brokkr has a small scar on his eyelid
cast.manner: Proud, gruff, finish each other's sentences
cast.note: Motive: "Our finest work!" They think Thor treats it like a ladle on a hook. · Secret: they promised Loki to tell nobody he came begging; they are bad at secrets and worse at lying

cast.name: Tooth-Gnasher and Tooth-Grinder
cast.look: Two shaggy grey goats with curling horns; one has a sock hanging from his mouth
cast.note: Motive: they chew everything. · Secret: they saw something in the night, and goats cannot say what

cast.name: Thrym
cast.look: Huge, frost-white beard plaited with gold rings, a cloak of white fur, arms improbably long; sits on a grassy mound
cast.manner: Vain, boastful, pleased with himself; not menacing, just very large and very sure
cast.note: Motive: he wants Freyja for his bride, and he thinks the hammer will buy her. · Secret: none worth the name; he cannot stop telling people things

cast.name: Thor
cast.look: Red-bearded, broad as a door, iron gloves tucked in his belt, a woollen night-cap he forgets he is wearing
cast.manner: Loud, honest, quick to temper, quicker to laugh

cast.name: Sif
cast.look: Long golden hair in one great plait, a keys-belt, a calm, watchful face

cast.name: Freyja
cast.look: Tall, a cloak of falcon feathers over her arm, a great necklace of gold at her throat
cast.manner: Proud, warm, and very sure of her own mind

cast.name: Heimdall
cast.look: Pale and tall, a great horn on a strap, eyes that never seem to blink
cast.manner: Quiet; speaks rarely, and then wisely

docs.title: Report
docs.author: Thor, as Sif wrote it down
docs.where: on a wax board at the hearth
docs.picture: a long wooden board with a wax face, a stylus on a thong, a pair of iron gloves dropped beside it.
docs.body:
THOR'S ACCOUNT
[[c:peg-under|Every night I hang my hammer on the peg under the smoke-hole, near the warm hearth.]]
[[c:barred|Last night I barred the door myself, from the inside.]]
[[c:fire-high|The fire was banked high all night.]]
[[c:roof-creak|Once, in the third watch, the roof creaked like a sea-steed's mast in a gale.]]
I thought it was the wind, and slept again.
[[c:woke-gone|I woke before dawn, and the peg was empty.]]
[[c:bar-still|The bar was still across the door.]]
Nobody in the hall heard a thing.
— Thor, son of Odin

docs.title: Note
docs.author: Sif
docs.where: pinned to the hammer peg with a bone pin
docs.picture: a strip of birch bark with neat scratched writing, pinned beside the empty peg; a glitter of white on the peg itself.
docs.body:
WHAT I FOUND
[[c:rime|There is rime on the hammer peg, white and feathery, though the hall is warm.]]
[[c:soot-stripe|The soot round the rim of the smoke-hole is wiped clean in one long stripe.]]
[[c:snow-floor|A little snow lies on the floor under the smoke-hole.]]
[[c:no-prints|Outside, the snow is smooth all round the hall. There is not one footprint.]]
[[c:wall-rime|On top of the north wall there is a long patch of rime, as long as a tree.]]
I have touched nothing.
— Sif

docs.title: List
docs.author: Sif
docs.where: the hall's day-tally, hanging by the door
docs.picture: a notched tally-stick and a strip of bark tied to it, written small.
docs.body:
WHO CAME TO THE HALL YESTERDAY
Morning: the goats were fed and shut in the stable.
Noon: a message from Brokkr and Sindri. "Is our hammer well? Is it polished?"
[[c:loki-dusk|Dusk: Loki came with a knotted cord. He measured the hammer's handle.]]
[[c:loki-nothing|When I asked why, he said, "Oh, nothing. Nothing at all."]]
[[c:thor-shouts|Evening: Thor told the whole feast where he hangs his hammer, again.]]
Night: the door barred. Everyone asleep.
— Sif

docs.title: Stave
docs.author: Thor, carved long ago
docs.where: a stave nailed beside the peg
docs.picture: a flat staff of ash wood with a column of plain runes cut down it; the live-text translation appears in a parchment box when tapped.
docs.body:
WHO CAN CARRY MY HAMMER FAR
Thor, in his iron gloves.
A giant, perhaps. Giants are strong.
[[c:dwarves-pole|The dwarves who made it, both together, slowly, with a pole.]]
[[c:goats-no|Not the goats. Pulling a cart is not carrying.]]
Nobody else in Asgard. I have watched them try.
[[c:rime-lore|Remember: frost-giants leave rime on whatever they touch.]]
[[c:north|Their land, Jötunheim, lies north, beyond the wall.]]

docs.title: Note
docs.author: Freyja
docs.where: tied to the collar of the falcon-feather cloak, which Loki carries over his arm
docs.picture: a cloak of brown-and-cream falcon feathers, folded; a small card of birch bark tied to it with a gold thread.
docs.body:
To Loki.
[[c:cloak-sunrise|I lend you my falcon cloak at sunrise, after Thor's roar woke all of Asgard.]]
[[c:cloak-once|It has not left my hall all night. It never does.]]
Fly quickly, and find the hammer.
Bring the cloak back with every feather.
I have counted them.
— Freyja

docs.title: Stave
docs.author: unknown
docs.where: stuck upright in the snow on top of the north wall, where no one could reach it from inside
docs.picture: a short peeled stick with six runes cut in it, frosted white; Dev's notebook beside it, open.
docs.body:
SIX RUNES, CUT DEEP
[[c:runes|ᚠ ᚱ ᛖ ᛁ ᛃ ᚨ]]
*Dev's working, in his notebook:*
F. R. E. I (they use it for Y). J. A.
[[c:freyja|FREYJA.]]
[[c:rune-why|Why would a thief leave a goddess's name?]]
[[c:rune-high|And how did it get up there? The wall is twice my height.]]

docs.title: Log
docs.author: the stable-keeper 🪔
docs.where: a slate on the stable door
docs.picture: a small slate with chalk lines, one corner bitten off.
docs.body:
GOATS, NIGHT
[[c:goats-latched|Shut in at dusk. Latch still down at dawn.]]
[[c:goats-ate|Eaten: one halter, one bucket handle, one of Thor's socks, and this corner of the slate.]]
[[c:goats-north|Since the third watch, both goats have stood with their noses to the north wall.]]
They will not stop staring. They will not stop chewing.
I do not know which is worse.

docs.title: Log (◆ appears at the start of chapter 4)
docs.author: Brokkr and Sindri
docs.when: last night, written as it happened
docs.where: carried to the Thing by Brokkr
docs.picture: a forge slate black with soot, chalk tallies down one side, a scorch mark in one corner.
docs.body:
FORGE SLATE, LAST NIGHT
[[c:slate-loki|Dusk: Loki came to the forge. He stayed until cockcrow. He never once left.]]
[[c:slate-cord|He showed us a knotted cord. "The handle is this long. Make Thor a longer one. A sorry-present."]]
[[c:slate-no|We said no. A Brokkr hammer is not changed.]]
He asked again. And again. All night.
Bellows working the whole time. No frost here, ever.
Cockcrow: he went away sad, with soot on his sleeve.
We promised to tell nobody.
— B. & S.

docs.title: Loki: Where were you last night?
docs.author: Loki
docs.body:
Here and there. Mostly there.
[[c:loki-there|"There" was warm, and noisy, and full of people who don't like me.]]
That describes most places, to be fair.

docs.title: Loki: Why did you measure the hammer's handle?
docs.author: Loki
docs.body:
Ah. Sif writes everything down. I admire that, mostly.
[[c:loki-cord|I was measuring it for a present. No. Forget I said present.]]
It was nothing. A very long nothing.

docs.title: Loki: When did you get the falcon cloak?
docs.author: Loki
docs.body:
At sunrise, after the roar. You heard the roar. Everyone heard the roar.
[[c:loki-no-cloak|Before that, I had no wings at all. Ask Freyja. She counts feathers.]]

docs.title: Loki: Who knew where Thor keeps his hammer?
docs.author: Loki
docs.body:
Who didn't? He tells every feast. Loudly. Twice.
[[c:loki-everyone|Every giant in Jötunheim could draw you a map of that peg.]]

docs.title: Loki: Why does everyone blame you?
docs.author: Loki
docs.body:
Because I'm usually guilty. I'm not offended. Usually is a fair word.
[[c:loki-handle|The hammer's short handle really is my fault. That was a long time ago, and involved a fly.]]
Today, though, I am only usually.

docs.title: Brokkr and Sindri: Did you make the hammer?
docs.author: Brokkr and Sindri
docs.body:
**BROKKR:** Made it! Our finest work!
**SINDRI:** And he hangs it on a peg. Like a ladle.
[[c:dw-pride|BROKKR: We have asked him to polish it. Twice. Yesterday, three times.]]

docs.title: Brokkr and Sindri: Where were you last night?
docs.author: Brokkr and Sindri
docs.body:
**SINDRI:** Here. At the forge. Working.
**BROKKR:** On nothing.
[[c:dw-nothing|SINDRI: On a handle. BROKKR: On NOTHING.]]

docs.title: Brokkr and Sindri: Could frost form in here?
docs.author: Brokkr and Sindri
docs.body:
**BROKKR:** Frost? In our forge?
[[c:dw-hot|SINDRI: Snow melts on our doorstep. Ice weeps at the sight of us.]]

docs.title: Brokkr and Sindri: Could you carry the hammer?
docs.author: Brokkr and Sindri
docs.body:
**BROKKR:** Together, on a pole, slowly. We did it once, to give it to the gods.
[[c:dw-tracks|SINDRI: And we'd leave tracks like two barrels rolling. Look at our feet.]]

docs.title: Tooth-Gnasher and Tooth-Grinder: Where were you last night?
docs.author: Tooth-Gnasher and Tooth-Grinder
docs.body:
*(Tooth-Grinder chews the end of Dev's scarf, thoughtfully.)*
*(Tooth-Gnasher looks at the latch, which is down. Then at {det}. Then at the latch again.)*

docs.title: Tooth-Gnasher and Tooth-Grinder: Did you see anything?
docs.author: Tooth-Gnasher and Tooth-Grinder
docs.body:
*(Both goats turn, slowly, and stare at the north wall of the stable. Their ears go flat.)*
[[c:goats-stare|They hold still, the way animals do when something very big went by in the dark.]]

docs.title: Tooth-Gnasher and Tooth-Grinder: Did you eat the hammer?
docs.author: Tooth-Gnasher and Tooth-Grinder
docs.body: *(Tooth-Gnasher looks deeply offended, and eats a bucket handle to make a point.)*

docs.title: Thrym: Do you have Thor's hammer?
docs.author: Thrym
docs.body:
Have it? I took it! Look at me, I'm delighted.
[[c:thrym-hid|I have hidden it eight miles under the earth.]]
[[c:thrym-price|No one gets it back unless Freyja is brought to me as my bride.]]

docs.title: Thrym: Can anyone find it?
docs.author: Thrym
docs.body:
[[c:thrym-brag|No one will ever find it. I am the cleverest giant who ever lived.]]
[[c:thrym-best|And Freyja will think I am the finest husband in all the worlds.]]

docs.title: Thrym: How did you get into Asgard?
docs.author: Thrym
docs.body:
Into it? Into Asgard?
[[c:thrym-feet|I never set one foot in Asgard. Feet are for little people.]]
*(He stretches. His arms go on, and on, like two pine trees.)*

docs.title: Thrym: Who told you where it was kept?
docs.author: Thrym
docs.body:
Thor did! He tells every feast. We hear him from here.
[[c:thrym-hint|But who tells giants things? Ask Loki. Loki is always telling.]]

docs.title: Thrym: When must Freyja come?
docs.author: Thrym
docs.body:
[[c:thrym-tonight|Tonight. The wedding feast is ready, and the mead is poured.]]
If no bride comes by dark, the hammer stays in the dark for good.

docs.title: Thrym: The persona question
docs.author: Thrym
docs.body:
Nobody taught me! I'm a natural.
[[c:thrym-reach|In the third watch, I was simply stretching. A giant may stretch.]]

questions.q: Why did you measure the hammer's handle?
When did you get the falcon cloak?
Who knew where Thor keeps his hammer?
How did you get into Asgard?
Who told you where it was kept?

perPersona.milo: So what you're actually saying is, you did it?
perPersona.signe: What happened in the third watch?
perPersona.hari: If I were you, what would I have   wanted?
perPersona.vani: You boast a lot. Who taught you to talk like that?

deductions.label: someone from the north
deductions.statement: There is rime on the hammer peg, though the fire burned high all night. Frost-giants leave rime on whatever they touch. A frost-giant's hand was on that peg.
deductions.why: rime is frost. In a warm hall it should not be there at all. One small, cold fact points out of Asgard, north, to Jötunheim. And it clears the dwarves, whose forge "melts snow on the doorstep".

deductions.label: the boast is a confession
deductions.statement: Thrym's boast mixes facts and opinions. The opinions: "No one will ever find it", "I am the cleverest giant". The facts: he hid the hammer eight miles under the earth, and the price is Freyja. Read literally, a boast tells you where, and why.
deductions.why: a boaster wants you to admire him, so he tells you too much. Sort what can be checked from what is only bragging: the brag is about Thrym; the facts are about the hammer. And the six runes on the wall were the price, left in advance.

deductions.label: Loki is cleared
deductions.statement: Loki had no wings until sunrise, and the hammer went in the third watch. And the dwarves' slate shows Loki at the forge from dusk until cockcrow, begging for a longer handle. His "nothing" was a present.
deductions.why: this is the season's lesson about fairness. "It's always Loki" is a reputation, and a reputation is not evidence. Every clue that pointed at Loki has an honest explanation, once the slate arrives.

deductions.label: the impossible thing
deductions.statement: Nobody came through the door: it was barred all night, and the snow is smooth. But the hammer hung right under the smoke-hole. The soot on the rim is wiped in one long stripe, snow fell through, and the roof creaked in the third watch. A giant who "never set one foot in Asgard" leaned over the north wall and reached down through the smoke-hole.
deductions.why: this clears Loki completely. Dev's theory needed someone inside to open the door. The door never opened. The thief never came in. Only his arm did.

wrongLinks.quill: Dusk and the third watch are hours apart. What was the cord for?

events.text: Loki measures the hammer's handle with a knotted cord
Loki arrives at the dwarves' forge, and stays
Thor bars the door; the hall sleeps
The roof creaks like a mast in a gale
The goats start staring at the north wall
Loki leaves the forge, sad, with soot on his sleeve
Thor wakes: the peg is empty, the bar still across
Freyja lends Loki the falcon cloak

shake.quill:
Could
Loki fly before Freyja lent him wings? Read her note: *when*?

feast.title: The feast (the explanations game)
knows: Thrym sent for her only this morning
the bride has hardly said a word.

items.prompt: THRYM: "Who ever saw a bride eat like that?"
options: She has eaten nothing for eight nights, so eager was she to come to Jötunheim.
items.answer: She has eaten nothing for eight nights, so eager was she to come to Jötunheim.
items.why: It explains the hunger and it flatters Thrym. "Always this hungry" clashes with "brides are usually shy". "Ill" clashes with a whole ox. True? No. The bride is Thor.

items.prompt: THRYM: "Why are Freyja's eyes so fierce? Fire burns from them!"
items.panel: lifting the veil to kiss the bride, and leaping back the length of the hall
options: She has not slept for eight nights, so eager was she to come to Jötunheim.
items.answer: She has not slept for eight nights, so eager was she to come to Jötunheim.
items.why: It explains red, burning eyes, and it flatters Thrym again. "Torchlight" would not make a giant leap back. "Angry" is the one reply that would stop the wedding. True? No.

feast.lesson: An explanation can fit every fact and still be false.

accusation.question: Who took the hammer? Where was it? And how did a thief take it from a barred hall?

options: eight miles under the earth, in Jötunheim
place.answer: eight miles under the earth, in Jötunheim

wrongSuspect.loki: Where was Loki from dusk until cockcrow? Read the forge slate. And when did he get his wings?
wrongSuspect.dwarves: Is there frost in a forge? And two dwarves with a pole: where are their tracks?
wrongSuspect.goats: Pulling a cart is not carrying. And the latch was down all night.

loki-let-him-in.quill: Show me the door that opened. Thor says the bar was still across it at dawn.
loki-let-him-in.name: Loki let the giant in

accusation.weakEvidence: You've shown a giant wanted the hammer. Now show how it left a barred hall with no footprints. Look up, {det}. What's in the roof?
accusation.note: Thrym, lord of the giants, who stood outside the north wall of Asgard in the third watch, reached down through the smoke-hole of Thor's hall, lifted the hammer off its peg, hid it eight miles under the earth, and asked for Freyja as its price. Nobody helped him.

reveal.text: Thrym took it. Nobody helped him.

reveal.direction: A murmur round the stones. Every head turns to Loki. Loki studies the moon.

reveal.text: First, the frost. There was rime on the hammer peg, in a warm hall. Thor's own stave says frost-giants leave rime on whatever they touch.
I carved that. Years ago. I'd forgotten.

Second, the boast. Thrym said he hid it eight miles under the earth, and the price was Freyja. "Cleverest giant who ever lived" is an opinion. "Eight miles under the earth" is a fact, and a confession.
And the runes on the wall. F-R-E-Y-J-A. He left his price before he asked it.

Then the impossible part. The door was barred all night, and the snow was smooth. Nobody came in. But the hammer hangs right under the smoke-hole, and the soot on its rim was wiped in one long stripe. Thrym said, "I never set one foot in Asgard." He didn't need to. He leaned over the north wall and reached down through the roof.
The rime on the wall. As long as a tree.
As long as an arm. And it was there from the very first page. Thor wrote: "In the third watch, the roof creaked like a sea-steed's mast in a gale."

reveal.direction: The stave with Thor's account rises beside the moon. The roof line glows. Beside it, Thrym's stretching arms, two pine trees long.

reveal.text: I thought it was the wind.
It was a giant leaning on your roof.

reveal.direction: The goats, at the edge of the stones, turn and stare north. Everyone finally understands what they were staring at.

reveal.text: And Loki. Loki had no wings until sunrise. He was at the forge from dusk until cockcrow. The cord measured the handle for a present.
We said no. He was very sad about it. It was almost nice to watch.
The short handle was my fault. I wanted to make it up to you. I'd rather be suspected than laughed at, usually.
reveal.direction: to Thor, not quite looking at him

reveal.text: It's a good handle. I'm used to it.
reveal.direction: a long pause; then he holds out the hammer, handle first

reveal.text: And you were right. Nobody is a thing to trade.
I read every story about Loki. I didn't read the page.

epilogue.text: The souvenir. By the standing stones, Freyja takes back her cloak and counts the feathers, all of them, while everyone waits. Then she plucks one, brown and cream, and gives it to {det}.
Now there's one fewer. I'll know where it went. The sky behind the stones is going pale. Sunrise. Dev pulls {det} through the Door.
The shelf. The falcon feather goes on the shelf by the Door, beside the tortoise-shell plectrum. Two of four places are filled. When you tap the feather, it stirs, as if in a wind from the north.
Dev's thread. Dev puts Runes and Riddles of the North back on the shelf, then takes it down again.
It's a good book. It just isn't evidence.
Whose turn is it to carry the torch?
There was a whole hall with a fire in it. I didn't need one.
Hands forward. Felix reads Loki's two replies from Dev's notebook.
"She has eaten nothing for eight nights." Footnote: it fits every fact Thrym had. Footnote to the footnote: none of it is true.
A clever excuse isn't a fact. I'm writing that on my hand.

Biscuit. Constable Tully is waiting in the office, out of breath. Biscuit is found in the dumbwaiter, asleep, with a white tea-towel over his head like a bridal veil. Nobody can explain the tea-towel.

The tune on the wind. As Dev closes the Door, the frost in its keyhole melts. The office is quiet. Then, from somewhere out on the dark quay, a violin plays four notes of a tune nobody in the agency knows. It stops before the fifth. The air by the window smells, very faintly, of violets.

epilogue.direction: Nobody answers. Down on the quay, the gas lamps are all lit, and the quay is empty.

drill.title: Kenning Cracker
drill.intro: Five riddle-names. Each kenning appears on a carved stave. The child drags it to the picture it names, then taps one word that explains the riddle.

items.proof: steed = a horse; a ship is ridden over the sea
whales travel on it, as people travel on a road
in the stories, Freyja weeps tears of gold

items.answer: all the words a person knows
items.proof: a hoard is a treasure store
a candle gives light; this one hangs in the sky
items.from: a modern riddle in the old style, made for this drill 🪔

marginNotes.text: Þrymskviða ("The Lay of Thrym") is a poem in the Poetic Edda, a collection of Old Norse poems that survives in one manuscript, the Codex Regius, written in Iceland around 1270. The poem begins: "Wild was Vingthor when he awoke, / And when his mighty hammer he missed." Vingthor is one of Thor's names.
marginNotes.source: The Poetic Edda, trans. Henry Adams Bellows (American-Scandinavian Foundation, 1923), "Thrymskvitha", stanza 1; Carolyne Larrington (trans.), The Poetic Edda (Oxford World's Classics, rev. 2014), introduction, on the Codex Regius. [VERIFY: the Bellows lines against the 1923 printing before ship.]

marginNotes.text: Why is Thor's hammer so short in the handle? In another old book, Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda (about 1220), the dwarf brothers are forging it while Loki, in the shape of a fly, bites Brokkr on the eyelid. Brokkr stops pumping the bellows for a moment to brush him away, and the handle comes out short.
marginNotes.source: Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Skáldskaparmál, ch. 35, trans. Anthony Faulkes (Everyman, 1987), pp. 96–97.

marginNotes.text: Old Norse and Old English poets often named a thing by a riddle-picture called a kenning: a ship is a "sea-steed"; the sea is a "whale-road"; gold is "Freyja's tears", because in the stories Freyja weeps tears of gold. Dev's favourite is word-hoard, the Old English kenning for all the words a person knows.
marginNotes.source: Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Skáldskaparmál, trans. Anthony Faulkes (Everyman, 1987), on kennings for gold and ships; Beowulf, line 10 (hronrād, "whale-road") and line 259 (wordhord), e.g. ed. R. D. Fulk et al., Klaeber's Beowulf (4th ed., 2008).

marginNotes.text: Some of the most ordinary words in English came from Old Norse, the language of the poem. They, sky, egg and window are all Viking-age borrowings. Window is the Old Norse vindauga, a "wind-eye": a hole in the roof or wall that let the wind in, like the smoke-hole in Thor's hall.
marginNotes.source: Oxford English Dictionary, "they", "sky", "egg", "window"; Merriam-Webster, "window" (from Old Norse vindauga).

marginNotes.text: (chapter 5 margin note, after Case Closed) Four days of the English week are named after gods of the North. Tuesday is Tiw's day, the god the Norse called Týr. Wednesday is Woden's day, which is Odin. Thursday is Thor's day: Thunor in Old English, the same word as thunder. Friday is Frigg's day (some scholars link it to Freyja instead). And Saturday? That one is Roman: Saturn's day.
marginNotes.source: Oxford English Dictionary, "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday"; Merriam-Webster, same entries.

exercises.prompt: "There is rime on the hammer peg, white and feathery." What is rime?
options: a kind of rhyme in a poem
exercises.explain: "White and feathery" on a cold peg tells you. Rime is frost. It sounds like rhyme, but it is spelt differently and means something else.

exercises.prompt: Put Thor's night in order, first to last.
options: He woke, and the peg was empty.
The roof creaked in the third watch.
answer: The roof creaked in the third watch.
He woke, and the peg was empty.
exercises.explain: Thor barred the door "last night", heard the creak in the middle of the night, and woke "before dawn".

exercises.prompt: Old poets called a ship a "sea-steed". A steed is a horse. Why call a ship a horse?
options: You ride it across the sea
exercises.answer: You ride it across the sea
exercises.explain: A kenning is a riddle-name. A horse carries you over land; a ship carries you over the sea.

exercises.prompt: Fact or opinion? "I am the cleverest giant who ever lived."
exercises.explain: Nobody could check it. It is what Thrym thinks of himself. A fact can be checked; a boast usually can't.

exercises.prompt: Thrym says, "Ask Loki. Loki is always telling." Is that a fact about last night, or an attempt to make you think something?
options: an attempt to make you think something
exercises.answer: an attempt to make you think something
exercises.explain: He gives no time, no place and no evidence. He wants you to suspect Loki. That is an insinuation, and it is not evidence.

exercises.prompt: Freyja writes: "It has not left my hall all night. It never does." What can you work out about her cloak?
options: Nobody flew with it during the night
Freyja flew with it at night
exercises.answer: Nobody flew with it during the night
exercises.explain: If the cloak stayed in her hall all night, no one wore it to fly anywhere in the dark. Ask what a line rules out, as well as what it says.

exercises.prompt: Thursday is named after a Norse god. In Old English his name was Thunor. Who is he?
exercises.explain: Thursday is "Thor's day". Thunor is the Old English form of his name, and the same word as thunder.

exercises.prompt: Two notes. A: "Dusk: Loki came. Never once left. Bellows working." B: "I was going to be mysterious!" Which is the dwarves' slate?
exercises.explain: The slate is short, plain and in order, like a work log. B is chatty and talks about the speaker's feelings: that is Loki's voice.

exercises.prompt: The bridesmaid says the bride "has eaten nothing for eight nights, so eager was she to come". It fits every fact Thrym has. Why is it still not true?
options: Because the bride is really Thor in disguise
Because Thrym ate the food first
Because eight nights is too short
exercises.answer: Because the bride is really Thor in disguise
exercises.explain: An explanation can fit every fact a listener knows and still be invented. Persuasion is built to fit what the listener knows, not what is true.

exercises.prompt: "The soot round the rim of the smoke-hole is wiped clean in one long stripe." What does a clean stripe in soot tell a detective?
options: Something long rubbed against the rim
The smoke-hole was swept for a feast
exercises.answer: Something long rubbed against the rim
exercises.explain: Soot comes off on whatever touches it. One long clean stripe means one long thing pressed along the rim, recently.

exercises.prompt: Window comes from Old Norse vindauga. What did vindauga mean?
exercises.explain: Vindr is wind and auga is eye. Early windows were open holes that let the wind in, like the smoke-hole in Thor's roof.

exercises.prompt: Make sense of this kenning in the old style: "the hammer-peg's thief reached down with his pine-arms". What are "pine-arms"?
options: arms as long as pine trees
exercises.answer: arms as long as pine trees
exercises.explain: Like a kenning, "pine-arms" joins two words into one picture. The arms are not wood; they are as long as pine trees.
